interview_question: During a working day, your team receives reports of incorrect search results, unusually slow file uploads, and occasional login failures. A recent deployment may be relevant, but the reports are incomplete and several teams are requesting attention. How would you investigate the problems and decide what to examine first?

A previous attempt to fix a dashboard calculation defect was unsuccessful. The issue still occurs for some users, although the original test case now passes. You have the earlier investigation notes, recent changes and a test environment. How would you approach the investigation now?

A service has begun returning intermittent errors. Application logs suggest a connection problem, but infrastructure monitoring shows no corresponding outage, and user reports describe different failure patterns. How would you investigate these conflicting signals?

A scheduled data-processing job sometimes finishes much later than expected. The delay does not occur consistently, and it is unclear whether the cause lies in incoming data, the processing code or an external dependency. What would your investigation involve?

Your team identifies a defect that affects a small number of users while also preparing a time-sensitive release. A quick patch is available, but it could interfere with another feature, and a more extensive change would delay the release. How would you decide what correction to make and how to proceed?

An error in a financial reporting application may produce incorrect figures in reports that customers rely on. One proposed fix changes a shared calculation component, while another limits the affected functionality until the problem is better understood. How would you evaluate the options and determine an appropriate correction?

A release includes changes to account permissions, search functionality and a background export process. Testing time is limited, and the team has identified different risks in each area. How would you organise verification before release and respond to unexpected test findings?

A software update changes the rules used to approve high-value transactions. The implementation passes the developer's initial tests, but an incorrect approval could have serious consequences. How would you assess whether the change is adequately verified before deployment?

A customer initially contacts support because an order confirmation has not arrived. During the conversation, they mention that their account also shows an unfamiliar delivery address, and they are unsure whether the order was placed successfully. How would you establish the nature and priority of the problem?

A customer returns after a previous support interaction failed to resolve repeated account lockouts. The earlier case notes say the issue was fixed, but the customer reports that the same problem happened again. How would you identify the actual problem and determine what information matters?

A customer reports several related billing discrepancies while also requesting an urgent account change. Some records are available through approved internal systems, but other information must come from the customer. How would you organise the information-gathering process while respecting the customer's privacy?

A customer believes a subscription cancellation did not take effect. The customer cannot recall the exact date, the account history is incomplete, and the available payment information does not clearly establish what happened. How would you gather and assess the information needed to investigate?

A customer asks to change the delivery address after placing an order. The order may already be moving through the fulfilment process, and the available options depend on its current status. How would you decide what resolution to offer?

A customer requests a refund because an electronic product appears to have stopped working. They have provided only a short description, and the purchase record is not immediately available. Several possible resolutions exist, depending on the circumstances. How would you decide what action is appropriate?

A customer is waiting for an investigation into a recurring service interruption. The technical team has not confirmed the cause or supplied a reliable resolution date. The customer wants a firm commitment. How would you communicate the situation and manage the follow-up?

A customer was promised an update on a complaint, but the promised contact did not happen and the underlying problem remains unresolved. You are now responsible for the case. How would you communicate with the customer and organise the next follow-up?

You have one available team and three competing tasks: a scheduled warehouse count, an urgent request to replenish stock for an active customer order, and equipment maintenance that may affect access to the warehouse. How would you establish priorities and adjust them if circumstances change?

An operations team must decide between continuing a time-sensitive delivery and stopping work to investigate a potential equipment safety concern. The available information is incomplete, and delaying the delivery would have substantial consequences. How would you determine the priorities?

A distribution centre has experienced several small stock discrepancies during routine daily checks. Operations have continued without interruption, but the discrepancies have appeared on multiple days. How would you assess the operational risks and determine an appropriate response?

A delivery partner reports that its capacity may be reduced next week, but cannot confirm how severely. Customer demand is also uncertain, and alternative transport arrangements have different costs and lead times. How would you assess and respond to the operational risk?

Two departments are preparing for a service launch. One reports that its work is complete, while the other says essential dependencies remain unresolved. Progress reports contain gaps and some dates conflict. How would you coordinate the teams and determine a defensible way forward?

A previous attempt to coordinate a site relocation failed because several handovers were missed. A revised schedule has been proposed, but some teams disagree about who owns the remaining tasks. How would you use the available evidence to coordinate the next attempt?

A facility monitoring system reports that operating conditions may be drifting outside the expected range, but some sensor readings are missing. The local team has not reported a problem. How would you monitor the situation and decide whether escalation is needed?

You are monitoring several active service activities with limited staff. One activity is approaching its deadline, another has recently developed a quality concern, and a third depends on information from an external partner. How would you track progress, identify changes requiring attention and decide when to escalate?
